entries.note: There is no shared threshold for a definition being reasonably clear or having been so for a long time.

entries.test: Compare public AGI definitions from early 2023 through publication for shifts from general cognitive competence toward economic criteria or existing capabilities.
entries.note: The surrounding examples give mission creep a concrete reading as changes in the criteria for declaring AGI.

entries.test: Public AGI definitions and declarations during 2025 would show whether substantial further shifts toward the alternative criteria described occurred.
entries.note: “We can expect” expresses a firm expectation here. The forecast period has ended.

entries.test: Compare OpenAI's published economic criteria and any documented 80% proposal with earlier field definitions requiring cognitive flexibility and resourcefulness.
entries.note: The normalization treats the 80% formulation as OpenAI's established definition; Marcus describes a suggestion and qualifies his recollection.

entries.test: The Information's reporting and public documentation of the Microsoft–OpenAI agreement would establish whether a $100 billion profit criterion was being considered.
entries.note: “Apparently” and “reportedly” preserve the evidential qualification rather than asserting an adopted definition.

entries.test: The proposed definition's wording and public financial evidence would show whether it omits cognitive requirements and whether iPhones had already generated $100 billion in profits.
entries.note: “Absurd” is evaluative, but the comparison makes a concrete, testable point despite its sarcastic presentation.

entries.test: Public evaluations of contemporary frontier models on factual biographies and legal grandmaster-level chess would establish their reliability on those tasks.
entries.note: Marcus denies competence across practically all qualifying tasks. “Cannot competently perform nearly any information task” can instead assert failure across almost all tasks and omits the original task restrictions.

entries.test: Public AGI essays, including Altman's referenced post, and successive definitions would show whether authors changed their criteria or discussed AGI without specifying criteria.
entries.note: In context, avoiding goalposts has the observable meaning of omitting a definition or criteria.
Marcus states his own acceptance criterion. The normalization broadens this into a general rule for when AGI should count as achieved.
Neither remarkable abilities and weaknesses nor their scope being well understood has a shared evidentiary threshold here. Marcus explicitly reendorses this jointly authored passage.

entries.test: Public deployment studies and reliability evaluations could compare demonstrated practical applications of contemporary systems with commonly advertised applications.
entries.note: The comparison is broad, but demonstrated usefulness versus public capability claims supplies a plain empirical test.

entries.test: Public evaluations and deployment evidence for successor systems would show whether they improved capabilities, expanded applications, and reduced weaknesses relative to systems current at publication.
entries.note: “No doubt” makes this a firm forecast. Successor generations have appeared by the evaluation date.

entries.test: Public capability evaluations available at publication would show whether contemporary technology supported an AGI claim under Marcus's stated human-comparable flexibility, resourcefulness, and reliability criteria.
entries.note: The source asserts an absence of justification. The normalization adds the stronger assertion that general intelligence has not been achieved.
